name: Notre-Dame Cathedral
about: Begun in 1613 as the Jesuit college church (architect Jean du Blocq): late Gothic in structure with Renaissance and Baroque ornament; it became the cathedral in 1870 and was greatly enlarged eastwards in 1935–38 by Hubert Schumacher. Pale yellow-grey sandstone walls and grey slate roofs; the skyline signature is two needle-thin dark spires at the east end plus a third, older west tower. The crypt holds the grand-ducal burial vault and the tomb of John the Blind.

photos.caption: Aerial view of the cathedral spires with the Gëlle Fra and Place de la Constitution
photos.author: Sophie Margue / European Commission

photos.caption: Drone shot of the cathedral from above
photos.author: Clemenspool

photos.caption: Exterior of the cathedral
photos.author: Zinneke

photos.caption: Exterior of the transept and choir
photos.author: GVR

interior.architects: Jesuit church begun 1613 (Jean du Blocq is usually credited with the design; Ulrich Job of Lucerne built it); carved organ gallery and portal by Daniel Muller (d. 1623). East extension 1935–38 by Hubert Schumacher.
interior.dates: First stone 7 May 1613, consecrated 17 Oct 1621 as the Jesuit college church; cathedral since 1870; enlarged eastwards 1935–38 (new transept, choir, east towers, crypt); west tower burned 1985 and was rebuilt.
interior.style: Late Gothic structure ("Jesuit Gothic") with Renaissance and Baroque ornament; the 1930s extension continues it in a sober historicist style.
interior.layout: Three-aisled hall church (aisles nearly as high as the nave) with galleries over the aisles in the old part; transept and long choir from 1935–38; three towers (old west tower, two slim east spires). Crypt under the 1930s choir.
interior.main_spaces: **Nave**: pale sandstone clustered piers carrying painted net/star rib vaults, Renaissance-carved gallery balustrades. **Organ gallery** (west): richly carved by Daniel Muller. **Choir**: tall stained-glass windows (mostly 20th c.), high altar. **Chapel of the Consolatrix Afflictorum**: the miraculous Virgin, focus of the Octave pilgrimage. **Crypt** (1930s): low hall on squat columns; the **grand-ducal burial vault** closed by a bronze gate guarded by two lions (sculptor Auguste Trémont); the **tomb of John the Blind**, King of Bohemia and Count of Luxembourg (d. 1346), with its sculpted mourners (remains moved here in 1945); bishops' tombstones; a small modern crypt chapel.
interior.materials_colours: Warm yellow-grey sandstone, white/cream plastered vault cells with painted ribs and ornament, dark oak furnishings, deep blue/red stained glass; crypt in grey stone with blue-tiled and starry details.
interior.access: Open daily, free (Mon–Sat 08:00–18:00, Sun 09:00–19:00, per the tourist office). Crypt usually accessible; closed during services.

name: Grand Ducal Palace
about: Built from 1572 as the city hall, extended in the 18th century and again in the 1890s, it has been the Grand Duke's town residence since 1890. The Renaissance façade is honey-coloured sandstone covered in fine geometric carving in a Spanish-Moorish-influenced style, with oriel turrets topped by slender slate spires and a steep dark roof with dormers. Guards in a sentry box stand at the door on the Rue du Marché-aux-Herbes.

photos.caption: Main façade from the Rue du Marché-aux-Herbes
photos.author: Moncle

photos.caption: Palace and the adjoining Chamber of Deputies
photos.author: Krzysztof Golik

photos.caption: Detail: windows, sgraffito and roof
photos.author: Krzysztof Golik

interior.architects: Original city hall 1572 (Renaissance façade); 1741 extension; 1890s renovation and new wing by Gédéon Bordiau (Belgian) and Charles Arendt (state architect).
interior.dates: City hall 1572–1795; prefecture 1795, seat of government 1817, governor's residence; grand-ducal residence since 1890; interior renovated 1883; looted under Nazi occupation (used as concert hall and tavern); redecorated in the 1960s; thoroughly restored 1991–96.
interior.style: Flemish/Spanish-influenced Renaissance façade with dense geometric carving; interiors 19th-century historicist (Louis XV/XVI revival, white and gold).
interior.floors: Ground floor (entrance, guard), **first floor = state rooms (piano nobile)**, upper floors with apartments; a 19th-century gangway links it to the Chamber of Deputies next door.
interior.main_rooms_(summer_tour_route): **Grand staircase** linking the state rooms. **Dining room** (state banquets): Napoleon-given tapestries, bronze and crystal chandeliers, ceiling with the arms of the twelve cantons. **King's Room / King's Lounge**: dark panelling, painted ceiling. **Map room**. **Reception hall / Ballroom**: white and gold, mirrors, chandeliers, balcony over the street. **Yellow Room** (the Grand Duke's Christmas message is filmed here). **Grand Duke's study**, and two private apartment areas at the end of the tour.
interior.materials_colours: Honey-coloured sandstone outside; inside white panelling with gilt mouldings, yellow and red silk, parquet, crystal chandeliers, tapestries.
interior.access: Guided tours only, in summer (2026: 18 July – 30 August, about 75 min, FR/EN/DE/LB, adults €18). Tickets from the Luxembourg City Tourist Office. **No photography inside.** Lift access. Also open on European Heritage Days.

photos.caption: Ballroom: white and gold panelling, mirrors, chandeliers

name: Chamber of Deputies
about: Hôtel de la Chambre, the parliament building, built 1858–1860 directly adjoining the Grand Ducal Palace. Neo-Renaissance façade in light sandstone with arched windows and decorative carving, flags at the entrance; much smaller and plainer than the palace next to it.

photos.caption: Façade of the parliament building
photos.author: Daderot

photos.caption: Exterior on the Rue du Marché-aux-Herbes
photos.author: Cayambe

photos.caption: Detail of the façade
photos.author: Daderot

interior.architect: Antoine Hartmann. Later annexes in the neighbouring buildings along the Rue du Marché-aux-Herbes and Rue de l'Eau.
interior.dates: Built 1858–60 next to the palace (to which it is linked by a gangway); renovated several times; during the Covid-19 pandemic (2020–21) the Chamber met in the Cercle Cité for distancing.
interior.main_rooms: **Plenary hall**: horseshoe of oak desks on red carpet facing the president's raised desk and tribune; tall windows with heavy curtains, faux-marble pilasters, crystal chandeliers, coffered ceiling with skylight, a public gallery on three sides with a carved balustrade. **Grand staircase** with red carpet and carved wooden balustrade. Committee rooms, corridors and a modern glass link, a members' bar, attic meeting rooms (all shown in the Commons category below).
interior.materials_colours: Warm wood, red and gold textiles, cream walls, marbled columns.
interior.access: Public sessions can be watched from the gallery; free guided visits for groups on request, and open days (European Heritage Days, e.g. 17 Oct 2026).

name: City Hall
about: City Hall on Place Guillaume II, built 1830–1838 in a sober neoclassical style on the site of the old Franciscan friary. Pale stone façade with a row of tall windows and a portico; two bronze lions guard the steps.

photos.caption: Neoclassical façade with its lions

photos.caption: City Hall, the square and the cathedral
photos.author: Cayambe

photos.caption: Corner view of the City Hall block
photos.author: Chabe01

interior.architect: Justin Remont (Liège). Bronze lions on the steps by Auguste Trémont (1930s).
interior.dates: Built 1830–38 on the site of the former Franciscan friary on Place Guillaume II (Knuedler).
interior.style: Neoclassical; two main storeys over a raised ground floor, cream render and sandstone dressings, hipped slate roof.
interior.main_rooms: Council chamber (municipal council meetings), reception hall / salle des fêtes on the first floor used for civil weddings and official receptions, mayor's offices.
interior.access: Not open to visitors; public council meetings; weddings; occasional open days.

name: Place Guillaume II
about: The Knuedler, the city's largest square, on the site of a former Franciscan friary (named after the friars' knotted belts). The equestrian statue of King-Grand Duke William II by Antonin Mercié stands in the middle, with the City Hall on one side. Used for markets and events; large paved open space framed by pastel town houses.

name: Place d'Armes
about: The old town's main café square, laid out in the 17th century as a parade ground for the garrison (hence the name). Lined with plane trees, with a bandstand used for summer concerts, and the Cercle Cité on its east side. Pink and grey paving, café terraces, a Christmas market in winter.

name: Cercle Cité
about: Cercle municipal, built 1904–1909 for city receptions and events, now Cercle Cité with exhibition rooms. Ornate Beaux-Arts style façade in cream stone facing Place d'Armes, with a clock under a sculpted pediment and a long relief frieze of Countess Ermesinde granting the city its charter of freedoms in 1244.

photos.author: Krzysztof Golik

interior.architects: Pierre Funck and his son Paul Funck (competition launched 1902, won 1904). Annex "Cité" (library, conference centre) added 2011, linked behind.
interior.dates: Built 1904–09 (some sources say 1904–05 for the shell); municipal palace from Sept 1909, inaugurated 1910; renovated and reopened as "Cercle Cité" in 2011.
interior.style: Neo-Baroque / Belle Époque, with a sculpted frieze (Countess Ermesinde granting the city charter) and a clock pediment on Place d'Armes.
interior.main_rooms: **Grande Salle** (ballroom): parquet, white stucco, mirrors, red curtains, chandeliers; used for receptions, concerts, the Chamber's sessions during its renovation. **Stair hall** under an oval **stained-glass dome**. **Vaulted gallery / foyer** with marble floor and a central glazed bay. Reception salons; the **Ratskeller** exhibition space (basement, free); conference rooms on the upper floor of the annex.
interior.materials_colours: Golden sandstone outside; inside white and cream stucco, marble, polished parquet, gilt details, coloured glass.
interior.access: Ratskeller exhibitions free, daily; the reception rooms on open days and events.

name: National Museum of History and Art
about: National Museum of Archaeology, History and Art on the Fëschmaart, the old fish market at the heart of the medieval town. Its main building (2002) is a smooth white limestone cube that goes deep into the rock, connected to restored historic town houses. Collections run from prehistory and Gallo-Roman mosaics to modern art.

interior.architects: New museum building by Christian Bauer & Associés (opened 2002), behind and below the historic Fish Market houses; later Wiltheim wing (2017) links the old houses.
interior.dates: Museum on this site since 1939 in old patrician houses; new wing 2002; Wiltheim wing 2017; reception renovated 2025.
interior.layout: A white natural-stone block on the Fish Market with a glazed hall; **three underground levels (about 700 m² each) dug into the rock** for archaeology; upper floors for fine arts and decorative arts (an Edward Steichen space planned on the 5th floor).
interior.main_spaces: **Prehistory level** in the rock (rock walls left visible, reconstructions); **Gallo-Roman level** with the **Vichten mosaic** (3rd c., the nine Muses) in its own room; medieval and coin rooms; painting galleries (dark walls, spot lighting); period rooms in the old houses.
interior.materials_colours: White limestone, bare rock, dark grey gallery walls, glass.
interior.access: Tue–Sun, free for the permanent collection.

name: Luxembourg City History Museum
local: Lëtzebuerg City Museum / Musée d'Histoire de la Ville
about: The Lëtzebuerg City Museum on the Rue du Saint-Esprit, opened 1996 in four restored town houses from the 17th to 19th centuries. Its large glass panoramic lift drops through the rock and has views over the Grund; inside, fortress models and the history of the city.

interior.dates: Opened 22 June 1996; renamed from Musée d'histoire de la Ville de Luxembourg in May 2017.
interior.layout: Four restored town houses (17th–19th c., medieval traces) on Rue du Saint-Esprit joined by a modern glass façade and atrium; the rock beneath was excavated for **four extra levels**, giving **eight levels** in all. A **glass panoramic lift** (up to 60–65 people) runs through all of them: rock foundations at the bottom, views over the Grund and the Rham plateau at the top.
interior.main_spaces: Rock-cut lower levels (archaeology, reconstructions), the permanent exhibition on the city's history through the floors, temporary-exhibition floors, the **city model / UNESCO visitor-centre room**, period rooms in the old houses.

name: St. Michael's Church
about: The oldest religious site in the city: a chapel of the counts' castle stood here from the late 10th century. The present church mixes Romanesque, Gothic and Baroque parts; it was rebuilt after the French siege, with a Baroque portal of the 1680s. Ochre walls, an onion-domed bell tower and a statue of Saint Michael with the dragon.

photos.author: Cayambe

interior.dates: Oldest religious site in the city: castle chapel of 987. Destroyed and rebuilt several times; present church mostly rebuilt in **1688** after the French siege, keeping older Romanesque/Gothic parts; baroque portal of the same period.
interior.style: Mix of Gothic (rib vaults, pointed windows) and Baroque (portal, altars).
interior.layout: Small hall church with nave and side aisle on round columns, rib-vaulted; west gallery with the organ; polygonal choir.
interior.main_features: Large **baroque high altar** (17th c.) with paintings and statues; side altar of the Madonna; organ gallery on columns; stained glass; St Michael statue.
interior.materials_colours: White walls and vaults, grey stone ribs and columns, dark gilded altars, coloured glass.

name: Casino Luxembourg – Forum of contemporary art
about: Built 1880–1882 as the 'Casino bourgeois', a society club where Franz Liszt gave his last concert in 1886; since 1996 the Casino Luxembourg – Forum d'art contemporain. Cream stone neo-Renaissance façade on Boulevard Roosevelt with a modern glass ground-floor extension.

interior.architects: Pierre Kemp and Pierre Funck (per the Casino's own history PDF; Wikipedia says Pierre and Paul Funck). 1959 glass pavilion ("Aquarium") by René Mailliet. Adapted for art in 1995 with Urs Raussmüller.
interior.dates: Built 1880–82 as the Casino Bourgeois (social club with ballroom and gaming); Franz Liszt gave his last recital here in July 1886; converted for European Capital of Culture 1995; contemporary art centre since 1996.
interior.style: Neo-Renaissance sandstone palace on Rue Notre-Dame/Boulevard Roosevelt; glass Aquarium (café/library) on the south.
interior.main_spaces: White-cube exhibition rooms on the ground and first floor inside the historic shell (ornate ceilings partly kept), the former ballroom, the Aquarium, a white stair/"Artgalerio" circuit, a black-box room in the basement.

name: Place de la Constitution
about: Square on the Beck bastion above the Pétrusse valley, home to the Gëlle Fra and the entrance to the Pétrusse casemates. Views of the Pont Adolphe and the Spuerkeess tower; site of the Christmas market and funfair wheel in winter.

name: Gëlle Fra
about: The Monument of Remembrance by sculptor Claus Cito, unveiled in 1923 for Luxembourgers who served in the First World War. A gilded bronze woman holding up a laurel wreath stands on a tall granite obelisk (about 21 m), with two bronze soldiers at the base. Pulled down by the Nazi occupiers in 1940, it was pieced back together and re-erected in 1985. The golden figure is a key colour accent on the Place de la Constitution.

name: Chemin de la Corniche
about: A promenade along the 17th-century rampart walls above the Grund, often called 'the most beautiful balcony in Europe'. Cobbled walkway, parapet walls and trees, with views over Neumünster Abbey, the Alzette and the Rham plateau.

name: Bock promontory
about: The rocky spur over the Alzette where Count Siegfried acquired the castle site of Lucilinburhuc in 963, the founding date of Luxembourg. The castle was demolished with the fortress after 1867; what remains are cliffs, casemate openings and the Schlassbréck (castle bridge). Yellow-brown sandstone cliffs with walls on top.

name: Bock Casemates
about: Galleries and gun chambers cut into the Bock rock, begun under Spanish rule in the 1640s and extended by Vauban and the Austrians in the 18th century; the whole city once had about 23 km of casemates, of which some 17 km survive. Raw yellow-brown sandstone tunnels, cannon embrasures opening onto the Alzette valley, and a stone bridge (the Schlassbréck) leading to them. Part of the UNESCO World Heritage site since 1994.

interior.dates: Galleries cut into the Bock rock from **1644** (Spanish), greatly extended under Vauban (after 1684) and the Austrians (1730s–1740s); at their peak 23 km of tunnels, about 17 km survive. Partly demolished after 1867; opened to the public in 1933.
interior.spaces: Rock-cut galleries on several levels with **cannon embrasures** opening onto the Alzette valley; stairs and shafts; the **Archaeological crypt** at the entrance with the foundations of Count Siegfried's castle (963).
interior.materials_colours: Raw yellow-grey Luxembourg sandstone, damp and dark, with modern lighting and steel walkways.

name: Pétrusse Casemates
about: Casemates dug in the 1640s under the Beck bastion, below today's Place de la Constitution, with staircases descending deep into the rock towards the Pétrusse valley. Closed for years for safety work, they reopened in the 2020s with new lighting. Rough sandstone vaults, steep narrow stairs and gun ports looking over the valley.

name: Three Towers Gate
local: Porte des Trois Tours / Dräi Tierm
about: The 'Three Towers' gate (Dräi Tierm, also Porte du Pfaffenthal) on the medieval walls: the innermost tower goes back to the city's first wall around 1050, the other two were added in the late Middle Ages. Three round sandstone towers with conical slate roofs, side by side over a gateway.

name: Spanish Turrets
about: Small stone sentry turrets (bartizans) with pointed roofs on the fortress walls, especially along the Montée de Pfaffenthal. Popularly called 'Spanish', though most date from later French and Austrian rebuilding. Pale stone with slate or metal caps, perched over steep drops.

name: Wenceslas Wall
about: Part of the city's late-14th-century ring wall built under Duke Wenceslas II, crossing the Alzette valley from the Bock to the Rham plateau. Stretches of rubble-stone wall with round towers, gateways and the Stierchen bridge survive; the 'Wenzel circular walk' follows it.

name: Grund lock and Stierchen bridge
local: Écluse du Grund / Pont du Stierchen
about: The Stierchen is a small medieval footbridge over the Alzette that forms part of the Wenceslas Wall, with a round tower at one end. Just upstream, the Grund lock (Écluse du Grund) was a fortress water barrier that could flood the valley. Stone arches, weir, rubble walls and the Bock cliffs behind.

name: Saint-Esprit Citadel
local: Citadelle du Saint-Esprit / Plateau du Saint-Esprit
about: The Saint-Esprit citadel, built under Vauban in the 1680s on the plateau above the Grund and the Pétrusse, on the site of a former convent. Its massive sloping walls drop to the valley; on top stands the Cité judiciaire, the courts complex built in the style of the old barracks.

name: Fort Obergrünewald
about: An 18th-century fort on the Grünewald slope between the Pfaffenthal and the Kirchberg plateau, part of the outer fortress. Low, thick stone walls, ditches and a caponier, partly restored, half hidden among trees above the Alzette.

name: Fort Thüngen / Three Acorns Museum
about: Fort Thüngen, built by the Austrians from 1732, named after commander Count Thüngen; its three round towers topped by stone acorns give the local name Dräi Eechelen ('three acorns'). Rebuilt in the 1990s–2000s, it houses the fortress and history museum since 2012. Grey-yellow stone towers with conical stone caps and gilt acorn finials, next to Mudam's glass roofs.

interior.dates: Fort built **1732–33** by the Austrians in front of the Grünewald front; named "Three Acorns" after the acorn finials on its three towers; mostly razed after 1867; walls rediscovered and **reconstructed** in the 1990s–2000s (alongside Mudam); museum opened **July 2012** (part of the MNAHA). Park by Michel Desvigne (2009).
interior.layout: Redoubt with three round towers on a bastion; the museum occupies the restored fort (vaulted rooms in the towers and curtain wall) plus a **new underground building** (exhibition hall and auditorium with glass floor panels showing the foundations), linked to the original **counter-mine galleries** that run under the glacis.
interior.main_spaces: Exhibition rooms on Luxembourg history 1443–1903 (cannons, models, maps); the long, narrow, lit **mine galleries**; auditorium; reconstructed casemates.
interior.materials_colours: Grey-yellow sandstone and limestone, bare rock galleries, modern dark interiors with glass.

name: Neumünster Abbey
about: Benedictine abbey moved to the Grund in the 16th century and rebuilt in the late 17th and early 18th centuries after fires and wars; later a prison (until 1984), it has been a cultural centre since 2004. Long ochre- and cream-plastered wings with grey slate roofs around a large paved courtyard, beside the Alzette and the Saint-Jean church, with the Corniche cliffs above.

photos.caption: Abbey buildings in the Grund
photos.author: Diego Delso

photos.caption: View over the Grund and the abbey at dawn
photos.author: Diego Delso

photos.caption: Abbey courtyard and buildings
photos.author: Dennis G. Jarvis

interior.dates: Benedictine abbey moved to the Grund after its predecessor on the Altmünster plateau was destroyed (1543); rebuilt 1688–1720 after a fire; after 1796 a military hospital, then **prison 1869–1985**; restored and opened as cultural centre (Centre culturel de rencontre) in 2004.
interior.layout: Four long wings around a large paved **courtyard (parvis)** by the Alzette, next to the church of Saint-Jean; cloister wing; gardens.
interior.main_rooms: **Agora Marcel Jullian** (494 m² covered courtyard under a filigree glass roof, the main entrance hall); **Salle Robert Krieps** (theatre/concert hall, 283 seats, former prison workshop); **cloister** with the Lucien Wercollier sculpture collection; **chapel** (baroque altar, stained glass); seminar rooms Nic Klecker and Lou Koster; brasserie; exhibition spaces.
interior.materials_colours: Ochre-yellow render, grey slate roofs, sandstone dressings; inside white plaster, stone floors, steel and glass in the new parts.
interior.access: Open daily, free (courtyard, Agora, cloister, exhibitions).

name: Church of St. John the Baptist, Grund
about: Church of St John the Baptist (Saint-Jean du Grund), the former abbey church of Neumünster, built in the early 18th century. Yellow-plastered walls, a tall slender black spire, and a rich Baroque interior with gilded altars and a Black Madonna.

interior.style: Baroque interior in a late-Gothic-shaped hall (pointed windows, rib vaults).
interior.main_features: Single nave with white vaults; large **baroque high altar** and side altars in black, gold and marble; **Black Madonna** (14th c.); **organ gallery** over the entrance with a historic organ; stained glass.

local: Musée national d'histoire naturelle / Natur Musée
about: National Museum of Natural History, in the former Hospice Saint-Jean in the Grund, beside the Alzette. White-plastered walls, slate roofs and a decorated Baroque stone portal with statues; the building's foundations sit right on the river.

interior.building: The former **Hospice Saint-Jean** in the Grund (17th–18th c. hospice buildings by the Alzette, next to Neimënster); baroque portal with the arms of Luxembourg and statues in niches.
interior.dates: Museum in this building since 1996 (permanent exhibition renewed since).
interior.layout: Long two-storey wings with dormered slate roofs around courtyards; exhibition halls on two floors, education rooms, café.

name: Adolphe Bridge
about: Stone road bridge over the Pétrusse valley, built 1900–1903 to a design by Paul Séjourné; its 85 m main arch was the largest stone arch in the world when finished. Pale sandstone, twin parallel arches joined by a deck, with smaller arches at each end. Renovated 2014–2017, when a suspended pedestrian and cycle deck was added underneath; the tram has crossed it since 2020.

name: Passerelle
about: The Old Viaduct (Passerelle, Al Bréck), built 1859–1861 to link the old town with the new railway station across the Pétrusse valley. About 290 m long with 24 sandstone arches, 45 m above the valley.

name: Grand Duchess Charlotte Bridge
about: Steel girder bridge built 1963–1966 (architect Egon Jux) linking the city centre with Kirchberg across the Alzette valley; about 355 m long and 74 m above the valley floor. Painted a strong red, hence the name Roud Bréck; it carries road and, since 2017, the tram, with glass safety screens along the sides.

about: Stone railway viaduct of the 1860s carrying the line north and east towards Germany across the Alzette valley between Pfaffenthal and Clausen. A long row of tall sandstone arches, now partly wooded around its feet.

name: Pfaffenthal Panoramic Lift
about: Panoramic glass lift opened in 2016, connecting the Pescatore park in the Ville Haute with the Pfaffenthal about 60–70 m below. A slim steel and glass tower with a footbridge at the top and a glass-floored viewing platform. Free and open late; one of the best views of the Alzette valley and Kirchberg.

about: The deep, green valley of the small Pétrusse river separating the old town from the Gare quarter, spanned by the Pont Adolphe and the Passerelle. Parks and paths along the bottom, sandstone cliffs and fortress walls on the north side; the river was renaturalised in the 2020s.

name: Municipal Park
about: Laid out from 1871 by French landscape architect Édouard André on the ground freed by the dismantling of the fortress, forming a green belt around the west of the old town. Winding paths, large trees, lawns and playgrounds; Villa Vauban stands in it.

about: A 19th-century villa built in 1873 on the remains of a Vauban fortification in the Municipal Park; the city's art museum since 1959, extended with a modern bronze-coloured wing in 2010. White façade, mansard slate roof, lawns and a fountain in front.

local: Banque et Caisse d'Épargne de l'État
about: Headquarters of the state savings bank (BCEE / Spuerkeess) on Place de Metz, built 1909–1913 by architect Jean-Pierre Koenig in a neo-Gothic and eclectic style. The landmark is its tall clock tower with a green copper spire, seen from the Pont Adolphe and the Pétrusse valley. Pale grey-yellow stone, steep slate roofs, carved ornament.

interior.style: Neo-Renaissance in a French manner with Art Nouveau touches; the tall **clock tower** with green copper cap is a city landmark.
interior.main_spaces: Monumental entrance hall and historic banking hall (not documented on Commons); **Musée de la Banque** (bank museum) inside the building: vaults, old teller counter, safes, calculating machines, history of savings in Luxembourg.

name: Luxembourg railway station
about: The main station building dates from 1907–1913, in a neo-Baroque style with a tall clock tower and a large arched main window. Cream sandstone with grey slate roofs and dark-green metal details; a modern glass entrance hall was added in front in the 2010s. Tram terminus and bus hub on the Place de la Gare.

interior.dates: Present building 1907–13; extended and modernised 2008–2012 and in the 2020s (new platforms and tracks 2021–25).
interior.style: Neo-Baroque (sometimes called "Mosel Baroque") with a tall clock tower.
interior.main_spaces: **Main hall**: tall barrel-like space, cream walls, arched windows, departure boards; **painted ceiling** (sky with a large sun and black linework); the large semicircular **stained-glass window** with the **silhouette of the old city** (towers and spires in warm yellows, reds and blues); the **glass-roofed passage** to the platforms; shops and ticket office.

about: Concert hall on Place de l'Europe by Christian de Portzamparc, opened 2005. An eye-shaped (elliptical) building wrapped in a screen of 823 thin white steel columns, with the main 1,500-seat hall inside. Bright white against the glass towers of Kirchberg.

interior.form: An eye-shaped (lens) plan wrapped by a screen of **823 white steel columns**; the foyer sits between the columns and the inner hall; two smaller halls are expressed as white sculptural volumes at the ends.
interior.main_rooms: **Grand Auditorium** (about 1,500 seats, max 1,471 in rental terms): shoebox with the audience in stacked "towers" of boxes around the stage, white and light timber, a high organ (Schuke, 2005). **Salle de Musique de Chambre** (about 300 seats): curved red walls, a white suspended canopy with star-like point lights. **Espace Découverte** (about 120 places, for electronic/experimental music and children). Foyer with long ramps and stairs behind the colonnade.
interior.materials_colours: White steel and glass outside; inside white, light wood, red (chamber hall), grey stone floors.

about: Museum of modern art by I. M. Pei, opened 2006, built on the foundations of Fort Thüngen's walls. Warm honey-coloured French limestone, faceted glass roofs and a central glass pyramid-like hall that echoes the fortress geometry.

name: Court of Justice of the European Union
local: Cour de justice de l'Union européenne
about: Court of Justice of the European Union. The original Palais (1973) has been extended several times, notably by Dominique Perrault, whose two gold-clad towers (2008) and third tower (2019) dominate the Kirchberg plateau. The towers and the Palais' ring are wrapped in bronze-gold anodised metal mesh.

photos.caption: Aerial view of the Court of Justice complex and Porte de l'Europe
photos.author: Sophie Margue / European Commission

interior.architects: Ancien Palais (1973): Jean-Paul Conzemius, François Jamagne and Michel Vanden Haute. Extensions (Anneau, two towers, Gallery; renovation of the Ancien Palais): **Dominique Perrault**, competition 1996, inaugurated Dec 2008; **third tower** (Perrault) completed 2019, the tallest building in Luxembourg.
interior.layout: The Ancien Palais (courtrooms of the Court of Justice) is wrapped by the **Anneau**, a ring raised on slender columns that holds the judges' chambers; the **Gallery**, a long glazed street, links the Palais, the three gold-clad towers (translation services) and the Erasmus, Thomas More and Themis annexes (General Court).
interior.main_rooms: **Grand courtroom** in the Ancien Palais: a huge canopy of bronze-anodised aluminium **gold metal mesh** (40 trapezoidal panels) over dark timber benches, interpreting booths around the top; other courtrooms in warm wood; **entrance hall** with black steel columns and flags; the Gallery (library, links); Rodin statue at the main stair.
interior.materials_colours: Gold/bronze mesh and anodised metal, dark wood, black steel, glass; outside rusty Cor-ten on the Anneau and gold-tinted glass towers.
interior.access: Public hearings are open to the public; free guided group visits on request (curia.europa.eu); open days.

about: The European Parliament's General Secretariat building in Kirchberg. The original 1970s building has been replaced by a large new complex completed in phases in the 2010s–2020s. Glass and metal façades in silver and grey with red window panels on parts of the older wings.

about: The national sports and cultural centre by architect Roger Taillibert, opened 2002: an arena and Olympic swimming pool under one huge, low, shell-shaped roof (the 'coque'). about: The central park of Kirchberg, part of the Kirchberg arboretum, laid out by landscape architect Peter Latz around d'Coque. Lawns, groves and straight paths with modern sculpture; d'Coque's roof and the Kirchberg towers form the backdrop.
